title: Why the police stopped him: Freedom Rides and the trip to Monroe
summary: He thinks police suspected the band of coming to cause disturbance during the Freedom Rides; they left early with two cars.

bands.name: Sugar Boy and His Cane Cutters

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did anybody get in trouble with your band or the police? No. I mean, did any groups when you were on the road have trouble getting black and white that we all get in trouble?
No, that's the only time that it would happen when I got hurt.
What, Rabinac was what you did?

No. Nope. You know, what I really think happened, the police stopped me and said I was speeding and I was drunk and they took me to jail. But what I really think it was, this happened in 1963. It was during the time they were having these Freedom Rides. And I was going to Monroe. This happened in North Louisiana. And I was going up there and I was pulling the trail. I had a trail on the back of my car. And I guess police must have thought we was coming up there to try to create some kind of disturbance. So it was about 11 o'clock in the morning when it happened. Oh, wasn't it night? No, it wasn't in the morning.
Oh, that kind of makes sense. And you know, you can think of somebody being drunk and speeding later at night.

Yeah, see, this is what happened. See, we left home, we left New Orleans. And the jail was, that happened on a Tuesday. And the jail was for 9 o'clock that Tuesday night. And we was in Monroe. We would have been up there for 11.30 that day. We could have stayed there all day, you know. We left home early that morning. Because nobody had anything to do. I said, okay, now let's leave early. Like maybe around 5, 5, 6 o'clock in the morning. And we could take our time, you know. Drive slow. You wouldn't have to worry about rushing. You know, we have a whole lot of time. So everybody agreed. So we just left, really. We left something like, like 5, I think around 5 o'clock, 4.30, 5 o'clock in the morning. We left. And we was in Monroe around 11 o'clock, you know. That's what happened. And we were.
There were more people than you in the car.
Yeah. It was, we had two cars and, you know. Had five, let's see, three, four, five, five people in my car.
So when the cops stopped you, it wasn't just you. I mean, he was out there, he was out there who bought the cops.
They had five people in my car and six people in the other car.
